content.title: Artemis II launch: NASA's first Moon mission since 1972 achieves successful lift-off — as it happened
content.text: NASA's Artemis II mission has achieved a successful lift-off, with the US space agency hoping to send humans around the Moon for the first time in more than 50 years.Four astronauts — including the first woman, first person of colour and first non-US citizen to travel beyond low Earth orbit — are now on board the Orion capsule Integrity, orbiting the Earth ahead of the next stage of their journey.Take a look back at how the launch unfolded below.Key EventsThu 2 AprThu 2 Apr 2026 at 1:32amThu 2 AprThu 2 Apr 2026 at 1:14amThu 2 AprThu 2 Apr 2026 at 1:07am2 Apr, 2:41amThu 2 Apr 2026 at 2:41amThanks for following our coverageBy Audrey CourtyThat's all for today — and what an incredible day it was!We watched NASA launch four astronauts on the first crewed lunar voyage in more than half a century.The 10-day flight around the Moon and back will put the spacecraft through its paces while venturing deeper into space than humans have ever gone.If the mission proceeds as planned, we expect the Artemis II crew to reach the neighborhood of the Moon on day six of the mission on April 7 (Australia time).Thanks again for following our coverage. You can read a complete account of the mission below:2 Apr, 2:27amThu 2 Apr 2026 at 2:27amAn uplifting story from one of our readersBy Andrew Thorpe My mum is a primary school teacher. I’m a PhD student working on moon missions (some of my friends in the US worked on this very one), so this morning I offered to live stream the launch for them and answer any questions the kids had. It was great, all of the year 1-4 kids piled into her classroom and they put it (and me, on the other side of the country) up on the big screen - the kids all did the countdown to blast-off together, and they asked great questions afterwards. Apparently they’re all still talking about it and are all excited and playing space games. The year 3-4s have space as a topic next month and are all buzzing about it now. Feels good to share the excitement I have for the next part of space, to help give back the way experts did for me back when I was that age. - JohnWhat a wonderful story, John — nothing captivates kids quite like space travel, in my experience. Thanks for sharing!2 Apr, 2:23amThu 2 Apr 2026 at 2:23amHow did they get through all the space junk?By Audrey CourtyHow did they get through all the space junk? - SueThanks for the question, Sue.Robert Howie, a space engineer at Curtin University, says the launch was "carefully planned" to avoid larger objects, which are tracked by the US Space Surveillance Network."The launch vehicle and spacecraft are also designed to withstand small impacts from natural debris such as small micrometeoroids and small artificial debris objects, such as flecks of paint," Dr Howie says.He adds that, for debris too small to track, they use a statistical approach to ensure the risk is below a certain probability threshold."The risk mitigation measures include the timing and path of the journey, the direction the spacecraft is pointing for different phases of the mission, and the structural design and materials used within the spacecraft," he says.2 Apr, 2:08amThu 2 Apr 2026 at 2:08amAdelaide company helping track Orion capsuleAdelaide-based aerospace Southern Launch will use ground-based infrastructure near Ceduna, on the Eyre Peninsula, to track the progression, speed and path of the capsule on the 10-day Artemis II mission.SA Space and Defence Minister Chris Picton watched the launch live alongside Southern Launch CEO Lloyd Damp, who called it "a momentous occasion".SA Space Minister Chris Picton with Southern Launch CEO Lloyd Damp. (ABC News: Isabella Carbone)"Southern Launch will measure the doppler coming off the Orion spacecraft, feed it back to NASA through our partners Raven Defence in the US, and help that spacecraft fly out to the moon. So, a very exciting day for us," Mr Damp said.Five South Australian staff will support the mission during its early and late phases.Southern Launch mission system lead Tyson Jones. (ABC News: Luke Pike)Southern Launch mission system lead Tyson Jones says it's "extremely exciting" to be working on Artemis II."I've been a big fan of space ever since I was a kid, so being able to actually work on something that's this close to it, even in whatever capacity we can, it's incredible," he said."I remember watching the video footage of the Apollo missions back in the day and being able to see it again now in my lifetime is incredible."2 Apr, 1:59amThu 2 Apr 2026 at 1:59amWhat will the astronauts do while they're up there?By Jacinta BowlerOur four astronauts won't be kicking back and relaxing on their trip around the Moon.On their first day in space, they'll be testing the systems on board the Orion spacecraft, ensuring everything is working as intended.After that, they'll take photos and analyse the lunar geography of the far side of the Moon, potentially providing new information about its southern polar region.It will be the first time some of the Moon's surface has been directly seen by humans.That said, the Moon won't look all that close, from their perspective — at about 6,000-to-9,000 kilometres away, it should look about the size of a basketball at arm's length.2 Apr, 1:54amThu 2 Apr 2026 at 1:54amOrion crew to practise 'proximity operations' with detached rocketBy Andrew ThorpeBy now, the Artemis II crew will have finished their initial set-up inside their spacecraft, making it liveable for the days ahead.Their next challenge is a demonstration of what NASA terms "proximity operations" — in other words, flying really close to another object in orbit.They're going to use the ICPS, the last stage of the SLS rocket to separate from the capsule, having just pushed it into a more distant orbit.There's a small (about 60 centimetres wide) target on the side of the ICPS, which the capsule will use to simulate docking.Here's what it looks like:(Supplied: X/@ulalaunch)The capsule will also be put through manoeuvres just metres from the ICPS, including an automated backflip and a series of adjustments using manual controls,In other words, this is pilot Victor Glover's time to shine.2 Apr, 1:46amThu 2 Apr 2026 at 1:46amHow you reacted to the launch todayBy Audrey CourtyHugo Scotty John: We did it guys we are going to make it to space today yes we did it half a step for spaceYOULLNEVERKNOW: This is coooolAdrian: Sounds like a very woke NASA mission.JJ: Did I just hear one of the crew say the dunny is busted? Oh dear ...PhilK: It has all been rather low key, not the usual big hype of a moon mission, but in a world gone crazy I'm sure the mission will deliver some great comedy with all the "flat earth" brigade claiming it's AI because of the glass dome nonsense or it's another Spielberg production. I just wish them well and a safe return.Emmie: We watched it before our year 10 assessment! Everyone was on the edge of their seats!2 Apr, 1:32amThu 2 Apr 2026 at 1:32amSo what's behind the new lunar race?By Audrey CourtyIn short, it's the discovery of water.After the end of the political "space race" between the United States and the USSR (now Russia) in the 1970s, expeditions to the Moon dwindled.It's only recently that interest has surged again, with countries like India, Russia and China also actively engaged in trying to land a spacecraft on the south pole region of the lunar surface.They've been spurred on by NASA's discovery of water molecules on the Moon.Areas of the Moon’s south pole with possible deposits of water ice, shown in blue. The map is based on data taken by NASA’s Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter. (Source: NASA)It's believed areas of possible water ice deposits could become a source of drinking water for moon exploration and could help cool equipment.It could also be broken down to produce hydrogen for fuel and oxygen to breathe, supporting missions to Mars or lunar mining.This means journeys to the Moon in the 21st century will focus more on creating lunar bases or satellites.2 Apr, 1:24amThu 2 Apr 2026 at 1:24amInternational Space Station crew sends good luck to Artemis IIBy Andrew Thorpe American astronaut Chris Williams, on the International Space Station, has posted a photo of Artemis II's rocket trail remnants, floating over Florida after the successful launch.While I would have loved to see a shot from the ISS of the Artemis rocket during its ascent, that was sadly not to be — the ISS was over the northern Pacific Ocean at the time, Williams says."Godspeed Artemis II! Our crew on the @Space_Station stayed up to watch the launch of our friends on their historic mission to the Moon," he writes on X."As we orbited a few hundred kilometres from Florida, I was able to catch a glimpse of the remnants of the trail the rocket made as it passed through the atmosphere! You can see the effect of the wind at different altitudes."(Supplied: X/@Astro_ChrisW)2 Apr, 1:14amThu 2 Apr 2026 at 1:14amArtemis II to replicate iconic Earthrise photoBy Audrey CourtyThe famous Earthrise photograph. (Supplied: NASA)Earthrise is the first image of our planet taken by astronauts circling the Moon.Asked whether the Artemis II astronauts have plans to replicate the iconic photo taken on Apollo 8, NASA's Dr Lori Glaze says: "Stay tuned ... We're gonna do everything we can to make that happen."NASA administrator Jared Isaacman added that additional camera technology had been packed to make the most of the opportunity to see both Earth and the Moon in the same shot.And that concludes the NASA press conference.In the meantime, do you know which year the Earthrise photo was taken? If you fancy yourself a bit of a Moon buff, then try our quiz below.2 Apr, 1:12amThu 2 Apr 2026 at 1:12amArtemis II astronauts set to break distance recordNorm Knight, director of NASA's Flight Operations Directorate, has confirmed that the Artemis II astronauts are on target to travel further from Earth than anyone before them — breaking the record set by Apollo 13 in 1970."Assuming all the burns go as planned and the timeline is executed as we think it's going to be, it'll be on flight day 6, at an MET [mission elapsed time] of about 18 hours," Knight says."That's where we will beat the Apollo distance record — or at least, that's where we believe that's gonna happen."That's in the small hours of Tuesday morning, Australian time!2 Apr, 1:07amThu 2 Apr 2026 at 1:07amTrump congratulates 'brave' astronautsBy Audrey CourtyUS President Donald Trump has opened his national address on Iran by congratulating the Artemis II crew first."It was quite something," he says."[The spacecraft] will be travelling further than any manned rocket has ever flown ... it's amazing."God bless them. These are brave people. They are unbelievable astronauts."2 Apr, 1:06amThu 2 Apr 2026 at 1:06amWho is NASA administrator Jared Isaacman?By Andrew ThorpeThere's a great deal of expertise and experience on display as part of NASA's expert panel right now.Administrator Jared Isaacman is definitely the odd man out, though.A commercial astronaut and billionaire who founded payment processor Shift4 Payments, Isaacman was first nominated to the position by US President Donald Trump in December 2024, despite no previous experience working for the space agency.He went through confirmation hearings in May last year, before his nomination was suddenly withdrawn, with many suspecting he had become a casualty of the president's feud with SpaceX founder Elon Musk.He was renominated on November last year and sworn in in December.(Supplied: nasa.gov)2 Apr, 12:57amThu 2 Apr 2026 at 12:57amSo what happened to the flight termination system during launch?By Andrew ThorpeThe NASA conference continues as I write.A journalist asks about the brief problem NASA experienced with Artemis II's flight termination system ahead of this morning's launch.To recap, the flight termination system is essentially a self-destruct mechanism installed on the rocket that NASA can trigger if things go wrong during launch and the launch stack poses a risk to populated areas.NASA associate administrator Amit Kshatriya says the system's communication link is tested ahead of the launch to ensure the self-destruct signal can indeed reach the spacecraft.It's an end-to-end test, meaning they need to receive confirmation from the flight termination system that it did indeed receive the test signal — and this morning, NASA "wasn't able to close that end-to-end loop".Kshatriya says the launch was ultimately saved by crews at the launch site, who switched to an older receiver and were able to confirm the on-board system was indeed sending back a signal."We had thought about getting a receive-only box that we had … and shipping that over to [the launch site] quickly, but they were able to fix it on the fly," he says."Once we were able to confirm that [self-destruct] command could get on board, then we'd met all our public safety risk [requirements]."2 Apr, 12:54amThu 2 Apr 2026 at 12:54amWhat are some of the key moments on the flight?By Audrey CourtyWhat are the major concerns as the capsule leaves its orbit and heads for the moon? Are there any key moments we should be watching for as milestones to know it's going to plan?- JesThanks for your question, Jes. The ABC Science team's Jacinta Bowler has the lowdown:"Most of the biggest concerns were in those first few minutes after lift-off. This, and the descent, are the two most dangerous times for a mission. Luckily, we won't have to worry about the landing for another nine days yet."As for important milestones, around three hours into the mission Integrity will separate from the upper stage of the rocket (the ICPS) and the astronauts will undertake a docking test by spinning themselves around."After a four-hour nap, the team will then be firing up the engines for the burn that will move them into a very high-Earth orbit and then on day two it's time to jet off to the Moon!"2 Apr, 12:48amThu 2 Apr 2026 at 12:48amAustralia to play key role in monitoring OrionBy Jacinta BowlerThe Canberra Deep Space Communication Complex is one of three facilities that make up NASA's Deep Space Network, which will monitor the spacecraft as it travels around the Moon.The three facilities are spread across the world, working together to ensure NASA can stay in constant contact with the spacecraft regardless of how far the Earth has rotated.There will still be about 41 minutes of communication blackout as Orion passes behind the Moon.The Canberra Deep Space Communication Complex. (Supplied: CSIRO/NASA)Australian astronaut and 2026 Australian of the Year Katherine Bennell-Pegg says that Canberra's role in the mission cements Australia's position as a key part of NASA's operations."In the Apollo era, Australia hosted the most amount of tracking stations outside of the US that supported Apollo," she said."We were absolutely critical then; we are also absolutely critical now."You can learn more about Australia's role in the Artemis program at the link below:2 Apr, 12:39amThu 2 Apr 2026 at 12:39amTesting Orion is 'paramount' for future Moon landingsBy Audrey CourtyNASA says it plans to launch rockets into space more often. (Reuters: Joe Skipper)A journalist has asked NASA administrator Jared Isaacman what success looks like for the Artemis II mission.Isaacman says understanding the Orion spacecraft is "paramount" for progressing to missions in which they actually land the capsule on the Moon."We've never flown Orion before with crew on board, so that's pretty important," he says."Every day we're getting data. It was mentioned from the get-go: this is a test mission."But we'll call success when [the astronauts] are in the water safely."In response to another question, he foreshadows "we're going to get back to the business of launching rockets in a regular cadence"."And we're going to bring the world along with us," he says.2 Apr, 12:36amThu 2 Apr 2026 at 12:36amOrion capsule completes important burnBy Andrew ThorpeA member of the NASA panel confirms that the Orion capsule has successfully completed its apogee raise burn during the press conference, extending the high point of its orbit so that its path is now quite elliptical.These burns are important, but they're small potatoes compared to the trans-lunar injection burn — the push that will send Integrity towards the moon — which is set to take place early tomorrow, Australian time.2 Apr, 12:27amThu 2 Apr 2026 at 12:27amTechnical issues were expected, NASA saysBy Andrew ThorpeNASA's panel is now taking questions from journalists, mostly focused on the technical issues that have come up so far in the mission.Dr Lori Glaze, the acting associate administrator for NASA's Exploration Systems Development Mission Directorate, says the space agency is still looking into the communciations issue that briefly cut Mission Control's ability to hear the crew.Another member of the panel mentions the toilet issues, as well as a water tank valve that closed itself during lift-off due to the G-forces.The vibe is very much "business of the day".Dr Glaze points out these sorts of issues are expected and are, in fact, the point of the Artemis II mission — to stress-test the Orion capsule under real conditions.2 Apr, 12:24amThu 2 Apr 2026 at 12:24amNASA: 'We know the challenges ahead'By Audrey CourtyNASA administrator Jared Isaacman says the four astronauts are now in the "capable hands" of mission control."They're safe, they're secure and they're in great spirits," he says."We've certainly been here before, we know the challenges ahead, we've got a lot of checkouts to get through."We will hold our celebrations until the crew is in their parachutes and splashes down off the west coast of the United States."
